title: Ashura: the fast of Musa
hookLine: the Prophet ﷺ fasted the tenth of Muharram in thanks for Musa's rescue (Bukhari)
last: A NEW YEAR FROM THE HIJRA.

lines: A NEW TOWN, A DAY OF FASTING.
cards: A newcomer has just arrived in a town, tired, after a dangerous journey. On one particular day, he notices that many of his new neighbors aren't eating. He asks why.
They tell him: this is the day God rescued Musa and his people from Pharaoh and drowned Pharaoh's army, and Musa fasted on this day in thanks, so we fast too.
According to Bukhari, that's roughly what happened when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina and saw the Jewish community fasting on the tenth day of the month.

teach.b: The day is called 'Ashura, from 'ashara, ten. It's the tenth of Muharram. Bukhari records Ibn 'Abbas describing the scene.

teach.h: WE HAVE A CLAIM TO MUSA TOO.
teach.b: The Prophet asked about the fast, heard the reason, and said that Muslims too had a claim to Musa, a bond with him. So he fasted that day, and told his companions to fast it.
Another report, from 'A'isha, says the Quraysh in Mecca had already fasted 'Ashura before Islam, and the Prophet had fasted it there.
Then, once the fast of Ramadan was made a duty, 'Ashura became optional: whoever wished to fast it fasted, and whoever wished to leave it left it.
A hadith in Muslim's collection says the fast of 'Ashura is hoped to wipe away the faults of the year before.
And another, also in Muslim, says that late in his life the Prophet resolved that if he lived another year he would fast the ninth as well.
He died before that year came, which is why some fast the ninth with the tenth, and some the tenth with the eleventh.
So among Sunni Muslims, the tenth of Muharram is mostly a day of fasting in gratitude, rooted in an older story: the sea opening, the people crossing, the army gone.
Tomorrow, the same date holds a very different memory, one that came later, and is kept with grief.

how: Many Sunni Muslims fast on the tenth of Muharram, often with the ninth or eleventh as well, as a voluntary fast of gratitude; the day is observed differently in Shia communities, as a day of mourning.

practice: Think of a time you were pulled out of something: an illness you recovered from, a mistake that turned out less badly than it could have, a person who showed up at the right moment. Stay with that memory for a moment.
If you pray, you can give thanks for it, the way the fast of 'Ashura gives thanks for a rescue.
